opus-5.5.text:
I think they're at quite different stages, and the gap is sometimes counterintuitive to people.

On the understanding side, you could say things have become fairly mature in a certain sense. If you give a model an image or a chart or a screenshot, it can describe it, answer questions about it, and read text inside it reasonably reliably. A lot of that progress came from connecting vision encoders to a strong language backbone. The language model already has rich world knowledge and reasoning ability, so once the visual signal is mapped into that space, you inherit a lot of capability for free. But "mature" comes with a caveat. When you push on fine-grained perception, like precise spatial relationships, counting, or reasoning over many steps within a visual scene, models still make mistakes a child wouldn't. So understanding is broadly usable, but its depth is uneven.

Generation feels more like a separate frontier. The visual quality of image and video generation has improved dramatically. Things look photorealistic, the aesthetics are good. But controllability and consistency are much harder. Can it follow a complex instruction exactly? Can it keep the same character and the same physical logic across frames? Can it edit one specific thing without disturbing everything else? That's where you see the gap. In a sense, generation has been optimized for looking good rather than for being grounded in understanding.

What I find most interesting is how the two relate. Historically they've been developed somewhat separately, with different architectures and different training objectives, diffusion on one side and autoregressive language modeling on the other. A big open question is whether unifying them really helps, whether a model that truly understands a scene will generate it better, and whether learning to generate improves understanding. My intuition is that there should be synergy, much like in language, where predicting the next token turned out to be a very powerful way to learn understanding. But in vision we haven't yet clearly demonstrated that kind of mutual reinforcement at scale. I think that's one of the more important things to figure out in the next phase.

r001.rationale: The response describes understanding as broadly usable and fairly mature, while calling generation a separate frontier with unresolved controllability and consistency challenges.

r002.rationale: It compares vision training with language next-token prediction and discusses whether unifying understanding and generation helps, but does not state that the understanding paradigm is less settled than the text-token paradigm.

r003.rationale: It mentions different architectures and objectives for generation, but does not attribute differences among companies’ techniques to the absence of a settled generation paradigm.

fable-5.1.text:
I think they're at pretty different stages, and the gap is bigger than people assume from the demos.

Multimodal understanding is, in a sense, further along, but mostly in the shallow part of the problem. If you give a model an image and ask "what's in this picture," or ask it to read a chart or a screenshot, it does fine. That's because we've essentially bolted vision onto a language model, and the language model is doing most of the reasoning. The visual side is just a good encoder feeding tokens in. So the understanding looks mature because it inherits all of the maturity of text models.

But the moment you ask for things that actually require seeing, not just captioning, it gets fragile. Counting objects, spatial relations, fine-grained reading of a diagram, understanding video over time, anything where you need to track state across frames. Those are not solved. And the reason is that the evaluation and the training signal are still text-shaped. We test understanding by asking questions in language and checking language answers. That biases the whole system toward "translate the image into words and then reason in words," which throws away a lot.

Generation is the opposite situation. Image generation and now video generation look spectacular, and the quality curve has been incredibly steep. But I'd call it less mature in the sense that it's less controllable and less grounded. The models are very good at producing plausible pixels and still not that good at obeying precise constraints, maintaining consistency, or respecting physics and causality over a long clip. A lot of the impressive outputs are selected. If you watch what fails, it fails in ways that reveal the model doesn't really have a world model behind it, it has a very good distribution over appearances.

The thing I find most interesting is that these two have been developed somewhat separately, with different architectures, diffusion on one side and autoregressive transformers on the other. And I think the real maturity milestone is when they are unified, where the same model that can understand a scene can also generate it, and generation becomes a form of reasoning. Like, if you want to plan a sequence of actions, you imagine the outcome. Humans do that. Right now generation models don't understand what they generate and understanding models can't generate to check their understanding.

So if you ask me to rank, I'd say understanding is more useful today, generation is more impressive today, and neither is mature in the deep sense. And I'd actually bet the biggest progress in the next couple of years comes from closing the loop between them, especially with agents, where the model has to act in a visual environment and get feedback. That's a much more honest test than any benchmark we have now.

r001.rationale: The response says understanding is further along and more useful today, but does not state that it is more systematically understood than generation.

r002.rationale: It describes understanding as relying on language models and text-shaped evaluation, but does not say its paradigm is less settled than the text-token paradigm.

r003.rationale: It notes that understanding and generation use different architectures, but does not attribute companies’ differing generation techniques to the lack of a settled paradigm.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate how impressive the results look from how mature the underlying capability is. Multimodal generation can be very striking: you see an image or a video, and you immediately get a sense of what the model can do. But producing something plausible is different from reliably following every constraint or maintaining consistency over time.

Understanding is harder to assess just by looking at a demo. A model might describe an image quite well, but does that mean it understands the spatial relationships, the causal relationships, or what would happen if you changed something? You need a task that tests those things. And when it gets an answer wrong, it can be difficult to tell whether the problem was perception or reasoning.

So I wouldn’t give a single ranking. For basic image recognition and question answering, understanding is relatively mature. For understanding a dynamic environment well enough to act in it, there’s still a substantial gap. Generation has made impressive progress in visual quality, but controllability and reliability are separate dimensions. I think the interesting next step is connecting the two: can a model generate something, examine the result, identify what’s wrong, and improve it?

sol-6.1.text:
I think multimodal understanding is currently more mature than multimodal generation, although maturity depends on what you want the system to do. For understanding, we already have a fairly useful interface: you give the model an image or a video, ask a question, and get a language response. That lets us reuse a lot of the capabilities and evaluation methods developed for language models.

Generation is harder to assess. An image or video can look very impressive, but that doesn’t necessarily mean the model can reliably follow detailed instructions. If you specify several objects, their relationships, and how they should change over time, maintaining all those constraints is still difficult. And if the result is wrong, making a precise correction without changing everything else is another challenge.

So I would distinguish impressive demonstrations from reliable tools. Multimodal generation has very impressive demonstrations. But in terms of controllability, consistency, and integration into a workflow, I think there’s still a larger gap. Understanding has its own limitations, especially with spatial reasoning and long videos, but it’s further along in becoming practically useful.
